observation: The apparent abnormality is in the upper-left cerebral region, but the final-SVM occlusion map shows its strongest positive support near the inferior central brain/skull boundary. Grad-CAM is also dominated by peripheral activation. Neither method convincingly localizes the apparent lesion, and no individual occlusion changed the predicted class.

Grad-CAM is dominated by activation along the inferior skull and outside the brain. The final-SVM occlusion map places its strongest hotspot within or immediately adjacent to the visible right-sided lesion, although the localization is coarse and includes an additional non-lesion region. Occlusion therefore provides more anatomically relevant evidence than Grad-CAM for this case.

The occlusion map’s strongest region overlaps the visible central lesion, whereas Grad-CAM is broader and includes substantial irrelevant facial and inferior anatomy. Occlusion provides the clearest lesion-related localization.

Grad-CAM, particularly Layer 4, strongly overlaps the visible right-sided mass. Although the occlusion map shows some response near the lesion, its strongest activation is at the inferior-right skull/image boundary, away from the tumor.

The occlusion map’s strongest response lies outside the right side of the head, with only weak scattered responses near the skull base. Layer 3 Grad-CAM shows some intracranial activation but remains diffuse and peripheral; it is still more anatomically relevant than occlusion.

Occlusion shows a strong response overlapping the visible posterior mass, but also contains substantial activation along the lower border and outside the right side of the head. Layer 4 Grad-CAM localizes the lesion more cleanly and specifically.

No lesion is present to localize. Occlusion sensitivity is distributed mainly across the superior brain, while Grad-CAM concentrates near the inferior image boundary; these maps may reflect features supporting the no-tumor decision rather than tumor localization.

No tumor is present for anatomical localization. Occlusion sensitivity is scattered across the brain but peaks at the inferior midline boundary, while Grad-CAM is also concentrated near or outside the lower image border. These patterns may represent features supporting the no-tumor classification.

The occlusion map includes some response near the sellar mass, but its strongest activation is posterior and away from the visible lesion. Layer 3 Grad-CAM is diffuse yet provides slightly better lesion-related coverage than the final-SVM occlusion map.

The true pituitary lesion is in the central sellar region, but both Grad-CAM and final-SVM occlusion predominantly emphasize facial anatomy and the right image boundary. Neither explanation convincingly localizes the visible lesion, consistent with the incorrect glioma classification.

The occlusion map produces a compact, strong response over the visible sellar/suprasellar lesion. Grad-CAM Layer 3 includes the lesion but is widely diffuse, while Layer 4 is predominantly off-lesion; therefore, occlusion provides the clearest localization.
